evidence_quotes.quote: We examine the role of custodianship in the renewal of the institution of public water services in Detroit, Michigan. Our longitudinal qualitative study begins prior to the 33,000 household water shutoffs of 2014 and follows this ongoing crisis through 2017.

In the early spring of 2014 the Detroit Water and Sewerage Department (DWSD) began to send tens of thousands of shutoff notices to roughly 130,000 households, half of its customers. These accounts were either 60 days or $150 past due (DWSD, 2014).
The work of individuals and groups to maintain the institution of public water services provides the context for this study as we ask: Who are institutional custodians and what evokes custodianship?
A total of 42 one-on-one semi-structured interviews were conducted between September 2013 and early 2015 (Table 2).
Formal-depth interview participants were those we theoretically identified as custodians, namely those proactively working to maintain or preserve institutionalized practices.

The last aspect of our model points to the intent, or intended outcome, of the custodians. We propose that efforts to restore the energy and resources (Scott, 2015) of a neglected and entropic institution is aimed at what we term institutional renewal.

For convert custodians concerned with access and affordability, a $4.5 million fund to assist low-income residents was an important aspect of the GLWA deal. However, with the fund over-subscribed and thousands still on shutoff lists, the water crisis continued well into 2018 (Stafford, 2018).

criterion_notes.c1: Yes (as empirical setting/context): the study is set in the 2014–2017 Detroit municipal water crisis involving mass household water shutoffs (33,000 disconnections in 2014) and affordability challenges in public drinking water and sewerage services (DWSD), although public water services serve as the context for studying organizational institutional custodianship.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording = yes; Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading = no. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper examines an institutional/governance factor in the organizational-theory sense—institutional custodianship, stakeholder mobilization, and institutional renewal of municipal public water services amid privatization threats. Under the binding 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, however, it does NOT empirically examine a rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement rules, or utility ownership/regulatory structure directly governing access). Instead, state emergency management, Chapter 9 bankruptcy, the 60-day/$150 arrears disconnection threshold, threatened DWSD privatization, GLWA restructuring, and the WRAP assistance program serve only as unanalysed crisis catalysts or brief postscript context, while the study's actual analyzed exposure is actor-level custodial types (operatives, warriors, converts, agnostics), personal motivations, discursive framing of broad values (labor rights, public commons, justice, health), and energizing/resourcing mobilization roles.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes: longitudinal qualitative empirical study (2013–2017) drawing on 42 formal semi-structured interviews, 48 informal interviews, 120+ hours of non-participant observation at 32 events, insider/investigator journals, and archival documents, coded inductively using Atlas.ti. Not excluded on qualitative methods grounds.
criterion_notes.c4: No: the primary empirically analyzed outcome is organizational 'institutional renewal' (how heterogeneous custodians restore energy, resources, and discursive support to counteract institutional entropy). Household disconnection totals, resident town-hall accounts of shutoff impacts, temporary 15- and 30-day moratoria, GLWA public retention, and the oversubscribed $4.5M WRAP fund are reported descriptively as crisis catalysts or in a brief two-paragraph summary citing secondary sources rather than evaluated as service-access outcomes of a legal/administrative rule.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes: population/sample (42 formally interviewed institutional custodians across union, NGO, community, corporate, and government roles in Detroit), exposure (heterogeneous custodial motivations, roles, and frame intersections), outcome (institutional renewal), and study design (longitudinal qualitative inductive case study) are all clearly identifiable, confirming that the exposure and analytical outcome lie in organizational institutional work rather than rule-type service-access governance.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes: full text is in English.

study_design: Longitudinal qualitative inductive case study (semi-structured interviews, non-participant observation, journals, and archival analysis)
population_and_sample: Institutional custodians active around public water services in Detroit, Michigan (42 formal semi-structured interviewees—11 operatives, 9 warriors, 14 converts, 8 agnostics across unions, DWSD/government, corporate water sector, environmental NGOs, and community groups—plus 48 informal interviewees and 32 observed events; unit of analysis: custodial actors and the institution of municipal public water services)
exposure: Heterogeneous institutional custodianship (actor characteristics, catalysts/motivations, energizing and resourcing roles—defender, reinforcer, reifier, replenisher, retooler, exalter—and normative framing intersections)
outcome: Institutional renewal of the neglected institution of public water services (restoring energy, resources, and coalition support against institutional entropy; with brief descriptive summary of GLWA public ownership retention, temporary moratoria, oversubscribed $4.5M WRAP fund, and ongoing shutoffs)
rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification (and lacking an analyzed household service-access outcome under Criterion 4). Although set during the 2014–2017 Detroit household water shutoffs and DWSD privatization debate, this Academy of Management Journal qualitative study empirically examines organizational 'institutional custodianship'—specifically who institutional custodians are (operatives, warriors, converts, agnostics), what motivates them, and how their energizing/resourcing roles and discursive value frames promote 'institutional renewal' against entropy. Rule-type legal/administrative mechanisms (emergency management, Chapter 9 bankruptcy, the 60-day/$150 arrears disconnection threshold, GLWA restructuring, and the WRAP subsidy fund) are treated only as unanalysed crisis catalysts or brief summary epilogue rather than empirically analyzed mechanisms governing household water access.
